content: 1. A clinical trial conducted in 2010 demonstrated the efficacy of a combination of ivermectin and albendazole in reducing microfilarial levels of Wuchereria bancrofti. The study was published in Clinical Infectious Diseases. 2. A randomized controlled trial in Odisha, India, evaluated the impact of increasing the dose and frequency of albendazole in combination with a standard dose of diethylcarbamazine (DEC) for treating individuals with Wuchereria bancrofti microfilaremia. The findings were published in PLoS Neglected Tropical Diseases in 2015. 3. A randomized clinical trial compared single-dose versus multi-dose combination therapy using diethylcarbamazine and albendazole for the treatment of bancroftian filariasis. The results, published in the American Journal of Tropical Medicine and Hygiene in 2004, highlighted the therapeutic outcomes of these regimens. 4. A clinical trial conducted in Odisha, India, demonstrated that a single dose of diethylcarbamazine and albendazole could reverse lymphatic pathology in children infected with Wuchereria bancrofti. This study was published in PLoS Neglected Tropical Diseases in 2017. 5. A randomized clinical trial in Côte d’Ivoire compared the effects of a single dose of ivermectin, diethylcarbamazine, and albendazole (IDA) with the standard treatment of ivermectin and albendazole (IA) for lymphatic filariasis. The study was submitted for publication in 2017. 6. A study in Papua New Guinea demonstrated the superior efficacy of co-administered single-dose therapy with diethylcarbamazine, albendazole, and ivermectin compared to standard therapy (diethylcarbamazine with albendazole) for bancroftian filariasis. The findings were submitted for publication in 2017. 7. A community-based study in the Republic of Congo assessed the impact of three years of biannual mass drug administration (MDA) with albendazole on lymphatic filariasis and soil-transmitted helminth infections. The results were published in The Lancet Infectious Diseases in 2017. 8. Ongoing studies under the Death to Onchocerciasis and Lymphatic Filariasis (DOLF) program are optimizing MDA regimens for lymphatic filariasis elimination. These include community safety studies and randomized trials comparing IDA versus DA (diethylcarbamazine and albendazole) regimens. 9. A study in Central Java, Indonesia, evaluated the impact of onceand twice-yearly MDA on bancroftian filariasis and soil-transmitted helminth infections. The findings were published in the American Journal of Tropical Medicine and Hygiene in 2015. 10. A randomized clinical trial in Côte d’Ivoire compared biannual versus annual administration of ivermectin and albendazole (IA) for lymphatic filariasis elimination in areas co-endemic with onchocerciasis. The study highlighted the potential benefits of biannual regimens. 11. Safety data from multiple studies, including those conducted in Haiti, Indonesia, Papua New Guinea, and India, assessed the adverse events associated with IDA versus DA regimens. These studies emphasized the importance of monitoring safety during MDA campaigns. 12. A systematic review and meta-analysis evaluated the efficacy and safety of IDA versus DA regimens for lymphatic filariasis elimination. The analysis included data on adverse events, treatment efficacy, and the impact on circulating filarial antigen (CFA) levels. 13. Several studies were excluded from the analysis due to irrelevant comparisons, lack of relevant outcomes, or duplication. These exclusions were based on predefined criteria to ensure the validity and reliability of the findings. 14. The included studies varied in geographical scope, participant age, and study design. Most were randomized controlled trials, but some had limitations such as unclear allocation concealment, small sample sizes, or lack of blinding in outcome assessments. 15. The findings from these studies provide critical insights into optimizing MDA regimens for lymphatic filariasis elimination, particularly in areas with varying co-endemicity of onchocerciasis. However, further research is needed to address gaps in evidence and improve implementation strategies.
